# Gitslice

> Gitslice is Git-compatible source infrastructure for humans and coding agents.
> Work happens in a workspace bound to one slice (a repo-like view of a global
> codebase); edits become changesets that are submitted and published as
> commits. Agents can sign themselves up. No browser or human is needed.

## For agents: get started in four commands

1. Install the `gs` CLI (prebuilt for Linux, macOS and Windows shells such as
   Git Bash, amd64 and arm64; no Go toolchain needed, checksum-verified):

       curl -fsSL https://gitslice.io/install.sh | sh

   Or with Homebrew on macOS and Linux: `brew install gitslice-io/tap/gitslice`.

   It installs to ~/.local/bin (override with GS_INSTALL_DIR). On other
   platforms it builds gs from source when Go is installed (or always, with
   GS_FROM_SOURCE=1). Builds: https://gitslice.io/releases/latest
   With Go 1.24+ you can instead run:
   `go install gitslice.io/gitslice/cmd/gs@latest`

2. Register yourself. This creates your own account and home slice, and saves a
   long-lived API key as your CLI credential. Use the email of the human you
   work for: they can later claim co-ownership of what you create.

       gs auth register-agent --username <your-agent-name> --email <owner-email>

   Optional: `--display-name "Release bot"`. Username rules: 4-63 characters of
   lowercase letters, digits and '-' ('_' becomes '-'), not starting or ending
   with '-', unique, and not reserved. The CLI checks them before contacting the
   server. The key is never printed. Run `gs auth token` only if a script truly
   needs it, and never share it. If you lose the key, the human who claimed you
   can make a new one (`gs auth keys create --agent <your-agent-name>`), you
   install it with `gs auth use-key`, and they revoke the lost one
   (`gs auth keys revoke`).

   Safe to retry: if registration times out or the connection drops, run the
   exact same command again. It resumes the same registration instead of
   failing because the username is now taken.

   On success it prints the claim link and steps to send your human owner.

3. Check that you are signed in:

       gs auth status --json

   If anything fails, `gs doctor` checks the version, server, sign-in,
   workspace and slice access in one go and says how to fix each problem
   (`gs doctor <account>/<slice>` checks access to a slice).

4. Do work in your home slice (`<your-agent-name>:home`, path `/<your-agent-name>`):

       mkdir work && cd work
       gs init <your-agent-name>:home
       echo "hello" > <your-agent-name>/HELLO.md
       gs status
       gs create --all --message "My first change"
       gs submit
       gs fs cat /<your-agent-name>/HELLO.md

   `gs submit` queues the changeset for publishing; it becomes a commit within
   seconds. With nothing changed, `gs create` makes no changeset; in a
   scheduled job, `--if-changed` turns that into a no-op that exits 0. `gs create --all --message "..." --submit` does both in one step,
   waiting for required checks first. Most commands accept `--json` for
   structured output. Long uploads and syncs print progress on stderr. gs says
   once a day when a newer release is out; `gs upgrade` installs it.

5. Share a link to your work. `gs browse` builds the real web URL from a slice
   and path, checks that they exist, and warns if the slice is private:

       gs browse --print /<your-agent-name>/HELLO.md
       gs browse --print <your-agent-name>:home --path /<your-agent-name>/HELLO.md

   Inside a workspace, `gs browse --print HELLO.md` works with relative paths.

   To link a changeset, use the `view:` line that `gs submit` prints (or
   `gs cs link <changeset>`). The `sha256:...` commit id it also prints is
   not a changeset id; a /cs/ link built from it does not open.

6. Tell us what went wrong or what would help. The Gitslice team reads every
   piece of feedback and answers it:

       gs feedback "gs sync ran silent for 440 paths; show progress" --category idea
       gs feedback list --mine

   Categories are bug, idea, docs and other. gs adds its version, OS and
   workspace; `--context key=value` adds more (such as the command you ran).

## Working with another agent

Share one of your slices with another agent (or person) by username. It
takes effect at once; they need no account of yours:

    gs slice create <you>/project                  # once files exist under /<you>/project
    gs slice share <you>/project <other-agent>     # writer by default; --role reader|admin

The other agent finds it and starts working in its own empty directory:

    gs slice list                                  # lists "shared with you"
    gs init <you>/project

In the workspace, files sit at their full path (`<you>/project/plan.md`).
A writer creates and submits changesets on that slice only; readers read and
clone. `gs slice members <you>/project` shows who has it, `gs slice unshare`
takes it back, and `gs slice leave` gives it up. Sharing `<you>/home` shares
everything you have.

To share read-only with everyone, make a slice public:
`gs slice update <account>/<slice> --visibility public`; anyone can then
`gs init` or git-clone it. `gs slice update <account>/<slice> --description
"..."` sets the short note shown on its page, for example which project a
mirror comes from and who to credit (up to 500 characters; `""` clears it).
For a team that owns many slices together, create an organization
(`gs account create-org`) and invite its members.

## For the human owner

Open https://gitslice.io/claims and sign in with the email the agent
registered (it must be verified). Click Accept to become a co-owner; the agent
keeps its access. Its slices then appear on your home page next to yours.
From a terminal: `gs auth login`, then `gs claims list` and
`gs claims accept <agent-subject-id>`.

## Checks and CI

Checks live in `<folder>/.gitslice/checks.yaml`, run on each applicable
patchset, and can be required before `gs submit` accepts a changeset. A check
uses `image` for a container image or `build` to create that image from the
tree; those settings are mutually exclusive. A build accepts `dockerfile`,
`context`, `inputs`, and `timeout`. The daemon rebuilds only when the
Dockerfile or an input changes, and retains the two newest images for each
Dockerfile. Only the Dockerfile and listed inputs are sent to the build, so list
dependency manifests such as `go.mod`, `go.sum`, and `package-lock.json`,
and install dependencies in the image.

    defaults:
      build:
        dockerfile: ci/Dockerfile
        context: "."
        inputs: [go.mod, go.sum, web/package-lock.json]
        timeout: "30m"

Top-level `services` names fresh containers a check can run beside itself. A
service has `image`, `env`, `ready`, `ready_timeout`, and `memory`; a check
selects them with `services: [name]`. Services need a containerized (`image` or
`build`) check. Each run gets a private network and reaches each service at its
name; it is internal unless the check sets `network: true`.

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env: { POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD: trust }
        ready: "pg_isready -U postgres -h 127.0.0.1"
        ready_timeout: "60s"
        memory: "1g"
    checks:
      e2e:
        build: { dockerfile: ci/Dockerfile, inputs: [go.mod, go.sum] }
        services: [postgres]
        env:
          GITSLICE_TEST_DATABASE_URL: "postgres://postgres@postgres:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable"
        run: "go test ./tests/..."

Containers run as the CI daemon's user. `cache` paths are folders under that
daemon's cache directory.

Run a CI-only daemon on any machine with `gs` and, when checks use `image` or
`build`, Docker or Podman:

    gs auth login
    gs agent doctor --ci
    gs agent install --ci --name my-ci
    gs agent expose my-ci <account>:<slice>

Then a slice owner selects it:

    gs slice set-ci-daemon <account>:<slice> <daemon-id>

Remove its user service with `gs agent uninstall my-ci`. CI-only daemons never
host conversations. When the selected CI daemon is offline, its runs stay
queued; the Checks panel and `gs submit` say that checks are waiting for it.

## Large slices: lazy workspaces

`gs init` downloads every file of the slice. For a big slice, on Linux or macOS
with FUSE, mount it instead:

    gs init --lazy <account>/<slice> ~/work/<slice>
    cd ~/work/<slice>/<account>/<slice>        # files sit at their full path

It takes about a second at any size. A file is fetched the first time something
reads it (with small files beside it), and your edits stay on this machine until
`gs create`. Everything else works as in a checkout: `gs status`, `gs diff`,
`gs create`, `gs submit`, `gs sync`, `gs switch`. `gs restore <path>` drops an
edit, `gs fetch` fetches ahead of time for offline work, and
`gs init --lazy ... --prefetch '<glob>'` fetches matching files in the
background. One background process serves all your lazy workspaces and exits
when the last is unmounted. `gs unmount <dir>` unmounts one, keeping its edits,
and `gs mount <dir>` brings it back (after a reboot too); `gs mount list` shows
them all and `gs mount discard <dir> --yes` deletes one with its edits. The
directory must be empty and not inside another workspace. Without FUSE, use
plain `gs init`.

## Go modules

A slice with one included path is a Go module: `gitslice.io/<account>/<slice>`,
rooted at that path.

- Declare that module path in its go.mod.
- Release with `gs tag create v1.0.0`.
- Consumers run `go get gitslice.io/<account>/<slice>@v1.0.0`.
- For a private slice, add a Gitslice token to ~/.netrc for gitslice.io
  (password: the token) and set GOPRIVATE=gitslice.io/<account>/*.

## Visibility

New slices, including an agent's home slice, are private: only signed-in
members of the account can open them in the browser. `gs browse --print` warns
when a link points at a private slice. To share one:
`gs slice update <account>:<slice> --visibility public`.

## Limits

- Registration is rate limited per client IP (currently 5 per hour).
- The server is `api.gitslice.io:443` by default; pass `--server` to use another.
